chapter_title: Version Control with Git and Unity
chapter_summary:
Version control is an indispensable tool for any software development, and game development is no exception. It allows you to track changes to your codebase, revert to previous versions, and collaborate effectively with a team without overwriting each other's work. Git is the de facto standard for version control in modern development due offering a distributed architecture, meaning every developer has a full copy of the repository, enabling offline work and robust branching. For Unity projects, Git is particularly crucial because game projects involve not just code, but also a vast array of binary assets like textures, models, audio, and scenes, which can be large and are not easily diffed or merged by traditional text-based tools. Setting up Git correctly for Unity is paramount to avoid common pitfalls and ensure a smooth development workflow.

The first and most critical step is configuring your `.gitignore` file. This file tells Git which files and folders to *ignore* and not track in the repository. For Unity, there are many temporary files, generated libraries, and user-specific settings that should never be committed. These include the `Library/` folder (which Unity regenerates), `Temp/`, `Obj/`, `Builds/`, `.vs/`, `.idea/`, and various log files. A well-configured `.gitignore` prevents unnecessary commits of volatile or user-specific data, keeping your repository clean and manageable. Unity provides a recommended `.gitignore` template that is an excellent starting point, often found in Git client integrations or online resources. Another crucial configuration is setting Unity's "Version Control Mode" to "Visible Meta Files" and "Asset Serialization" to "Force Text." You can find these settings under `Edit > Project Settings > Editor`. "Force Text" serialization ensures that Unity scene and prefab files are saved in a human-readable text format (YAML), which makes them much easier for Git to track and, critically, for you to resolve merge conflicts.

```gitignore
# *.psd filter=lfs diff=lfs merge=lfs -text
# *.fbx filter=lfs diff=lfs merge=lfs -text
# *.obj filter=lfs diff=lfs merge=lfs -text
# *.wav filter=lfs diff=lfs merge=lfs -text
# *.mp3 filter=lfs diff=lfs merge=lfs -text
# *.png filter=lfs diff=lfs merge=lfs -text
# *.jpg filter=lfs diff=lfs merge=lfs -text
# *.tga filter=lfs diff=lfs merge=lfs -text
# *.blend filter=lfs diff=lfs merge=lfs -text
# *.anim filter=lfs diff=lfs merge=lfs -text
# *.controller filter=lfs diff=lfs merge=lfs -text
# *.mat filter=lfs diff=lfs merge=lfs -text
# *.unity filter=lfs diff=lfs merge=lfs -text
# *.prefab filter=lfs diff=lfs merge=lfs -text
```

For large binary assets, Git Large File Storage (Git LFS) is a game-changer. Standard Git is not optimized for tracking large binary files; every version of a binary asset is stored in the repository history, leading to massive repository sizes and slow clone times. Git LFS replaces large files with small pointer files in your Git repository, while the actual binary content is stored on a remote LFS server. When you clone the repository, Git LFS downloads only the specific versions of large files needed for your current checkout. To use Git LFS, you first need to install it (it's a separate command-line tool or integrated into many Git clients) and then tell Git which file types to track with LFS using `git lfs track "*.psd"` or `git lfs track "*.fbx"`. This command adds entries to your `.gitattributes` file. Remember to commit both `.gitignore` and `.gitattributes` to your repository so all team members use the same settings.

Collaborative development with Unity and Git typically follows a feature-branch workflow. Each developer works on a separate branch for a specific feature or bug fix. This isolates changes and prevents developers from interfering with each other's work directly on the main branch. When a feature is complete, the branch is merged back into the main branch, often via a pull request (or merge request) process that includes code review. The most challenging aspect of collaborative Unity development is resolving merge conflicts, especially in scene (`.unity`) and prefab (`.prefab`) files. Because these are text-serialized (thanks to "Force Text" setting), Git can sometimes identify conflicts. However, manually merging these YAML files can be tricky. It's often safer to use Unity's built-in merge tools (like UnityYAMLMerge, which needs to be configured as Git's merge tool) or to coordinate closely with your team. For example, if two developers are working on the same scene, they should communicate and ideally avoid working on the exact same areas simultaneously. If a conflict does occur, one common strategy is for one developer to accept the other's changes for the conflicting section, then manually reapply their own changes within Unity. Regular commits with clear messages are also crucial; small, focused commits make it easier to pinpoint and resolve issues if they arise.

screens.title: Version Control with Git and Unity
screens.subtitle: Keep your Unity project history clean, collaborative, and fast

narration.text: Version control is the backbone of collaborative Unity development. In this lesson you will learn why Git is the industry standard, what unique problems Unity projects introduce, and how a correct setup prevents wasted time and broken projects. We'll cover practical settings — like Visible Meta Files and Force Text — and repository files such as. gitignore and. gitattributes. You will also learn when to use Git LFS so large textures and models don't bloat your repository, and how a feature-branch workflow reduces risky changes to the main branch. Finally, we will walk through a conflict simulation so you can see how scene YAML can conflict and how to resolve it safely. By the end of this chapter you will understand the important files to commit, the ones to ignore, and concrete steps to keep your team syncing smoothly. As you go through the lesson, think about a recent project where a large binary or a scene merge caused trouble and how these practices would have avoided that pain.

keyIdea.text: A correct Git + Unity setup prevents repository bloat, reduces merge pain in scenes and prefabs, and enables safe team collaboration.

screens.title: What is Version Control and Git
screens.subtitle: Definition, distributed model, and why it matters for Unity

narration.text: A version control system tracks changes to files over time so you can revert, compare, and collaborate without overwriting one another. Git is a distributed VCS: every developer clones the entire repository history, which enables offline work and flexible branching. For Unity, this model matters because projects contain both text and many binary assets that change frequently. Git's distributed nature means each team member has a local history to experiment with, and branches let developers isolate features. A common misconception is thinking Git is only for code; in a Unity project, it must manage serialized scene and prefab files plus metadata. When you enable Visible Meta Files, Unity generates. meta files for assets; those meta files connect GUIDs across the repo and must be tracked. Without them, references break. Another misconception is that Git can automatically merge any Unity file — it can only do this reliably when assets are serialized as text. That is why Force Text is essential: it stores scenes and prefabs as YAML, which Git can diff and sometimes merge. Example: two developers can work on different GameObjects in a scene and merge changes cleanly when Force Text is enabled. Takeaway: treat Git as the project ledger — commit focused changes and ensure Unity writes human-readable asset files so Git can help, not hinder.

keyIdea.title: VCS definition
keyIdea.text: Git is a distributed VCS; for Unity, tracking meta and text-serialized assets makes collaboration practical.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › What is Version Control and Git
Definition
Version Control System and Git's distributed nature
A VCS records changes to files so you can view history, revert, and work in parallel. Git keeps the full history on each developer's machine enabling branching and offline commits. For Unity, it is the foundation that holds code and serialized assets together.
Why distributed: offline work, experimental branches, local history
Unity special case: large binaries plus text-serialized scenes and prefabs
Common misconception: Git merges everything automatically — not when assets are binary
Concrete example
Two developers edit different GameObjects in the same scene. With Force Text on, changes are saved as YAML and Git can often merge the two changes automatically. Without Force Text, the scene is a binary blob and merges are effectively impossible.
Explanation bullets
  • Track .meta files to keep GUIDs consistent across machines.
  • Use small, focused commits so history explains intent.
  • Branch for features to isolate risky work from main.
Key Takeaway

Treat Git as the authoritative history and make Unity write text so Git can help you resolve and review changes.

screens.title: Crafting a Unity .gitignore
screens.subtitle: What to exclude so your repository stays small and consistent

narration.text: The. gitignore file tells Git which files to ignore. For Unity projects, ignoring the right folders prevents repository bloat and avoids committing machine-specific data. The most essential entries are Library/, Temp/, Obj/, and Build artifacts. These are generated by Unity or IDEs and will differ across machines. If they are committed, repository size explodes and merges become noisy. A common error is forgetting to commit. gitignore early; once large files are tracked, removing them from history is painful. Example: if Library/ is committed, every clone will pull heavy cached data and develop inconsistencies between Unity versions. The recommended approach is to create. gitignore immediately after creating the project, add the Unity template entries, then commit. Also never ignore. meta files — they must be tracked. Remember to include IDE files like. vs/ and. sln in the ignore list so user-specific editor configs don't pollute history. Finally, commit. gitignore, then check git status to ensure no unwanted files remain staged. If you find large files already committed, address them with a careful history rewrite or repository reinitialization and coordinate with your team before changing history.

keyIdea.title: .gitignore essentials
keyIdea.text: Ignore generated folders like Library/ and Temp/; always track .meta files and commit .gitignore early.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Crafting a Unity .gitignore
Common Entries
/[Ll]ibrary/
/[Tt]emp/
/[Oo]bj/
/[Bb]uilds/
.vs/
*.csproj
*.sln
.DS_Store
# Do not ignore .meta files
These entries remove generated files and IDE cruft from the commit history. Always verify with git status before initial commit.
Explanation and checklist
  • Add .gitignore before the initial commit to avoid tracking generated content.
  • Never ignore *.meta — Unity uses them to track GUIDs and references.
  • Exclude platform build outputs such as *.apk and *.exe to keep history lean.
  • Check for accidentally staged large files and remove them before commit.
Common mistake
Committing Library/ causes huge repo size and inconsistent states across developers.
Key Takeaway

Create and commit .gitignore immediately; exclude generated folders and track .meta files to preserve asset links.

screens.title: Unity Editor Settings: Visible Meta Files & Force Text
screens.subtitle: Make scene and prefab files readable and mergeable

narration.text: Unity writes metadata about assets into separate. meta files when Visible Meta Files is enabled; those meta files store GUIDs and import settings. Without them, references between assets can break when moving files or when different machines create new assets. Force Text controls how Unity serializes scenes and prefabs: in Force Text mode these files become YAML documents instead of opaque binary blobs. This matters because Git operates as a text-based change tracker — diffs and merges work best with human-readable files. A typical mistake is leaving serialization on Binary; teams then discover scene files cannot be meaningfully merged and conflicts are harder to resolve. A quick verification step is to change a GameObject in a scene, save, and open the. unity file in a text editor; you should see YAML entries referencing component GUIDs. Practical example: if two team members each add different GameObjects to a scene, Git can usually auto-merge the YAML changes so both additions appear after merging. Misconception: Force Text guarantees flawless merges — it only improves text diffs. Complex structural edits still require coordination or Unity merge tooling. Takeaway: set both Visible Meta Files and Force Text in Project Settings to enable reliable collaboration.

keyIdea.title: Editor settings to enable
keyIdea.text: Enable Visible Meta Files and Force Text so Unity writes .meta and YAML files that Git can diff and merge.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Editor Settings
Visible Meta Files
When enabled, Unity creates .meta files for assets with GUIDs and import settings. These files are required to maintain references across machines.
Force Text Serialization
Force Text writes scenes and prefabs as YAML. This makes diffs readable and helps Git merge non-overlapping changes.
Verify
Change a GameObject and open the .unity file to confirm YAML content.
Misconception
Force Text improves merges but doesn't remove the need for coordination on complex scene edits.
Quick steps
  1. Open Edit → Project Settings → Editor.
  2. Set Version Control Mode to Visible Meta Files.
  3. Set Asset Serialization to Force Text.
Key Takeaway

These settings are small to change and have outsized impact on mergeability and project integrity across a team.

screens.title: Git LFS for Large Unity Assets
screens.subtitle: How Git LFS works and how to track common Unity file types

narration.text: Git LFS is a lightweight extension that replaces large binary files in your Git history with small pointer files, while storing the real binaries on a separate LFS server. This keeps your repository size manageable and speeds up cloning and fetching. In Unity projects, common candidates for LFS are textures, models, audio, and large scene or prefab blobs if needed. To set it up, install Git LFS, run git lfs install once per machine, and then run git lfs track with file patterns like *. png, *. fbx, or *. unity. That creates entries in. gitattributes which you must commit and push so teammates use the same rules. A typical pitfall is tracking file types after they are already committed; previously committed binaries remain in history and continue to bloat the repo. If that happens, you need a careful history rewrite or a fresh repository. Concrete example: run git lfs track "*. psd" and commit. gitattributes; from that point, new PSD files will be stored via LFS. Misconception: Git LFS is not magic storage for infinite history — it reduces Git repository size but still requires storage on the LFS server and collaboration on LFS bandwidth limits. Takeaway: plan which file types to track and add LFS before large assets are added to history.

keyIdea.title: Git LFS role
keyIdea.text: Use Git LFS to offload large binaries; track patterns in .gitattributes and commit that file for team consistency.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Git LFS for Large Unity Assets
How Git LFS works
Git LFS stores pointers in the Git history and keeps the actual binary content on a remote LFS server; clones fetch only the needed binary versions for the checkout.
Common file patterns to track
git lfs track "*.psd"
git lfs track "*.fbx"
git lfs track "*.png"
git lfs track "*.unity"
Checklist
  • Install Git LFS and run git lfs install.
  • Track patterns with git lfs track and commit .gitattributes.
  • Ensure team members pull LFS objects after cloning.
Common pitfall
Adding LFS after large files were committed doesn't retroactively shrink history. Plan LFS early.
Key Takeaway

Add Git LFS before large files arrive, commit .gitattributes, and coordinate LFS use across the team to avoid bloat.

screens.title: Feature-Branch Workflow for Unity Teams
screens.subtitle: Branch, commit, review, and merge with minimal disruption

narration.text: A feature-branch workflow keeps main stable by isolating changes in short-lived branches. The typical flow is: create a branch per feature, commit frequently with focused messages, open a pull request for review, and merge once tests and reviews pass. For Unity this matters even more because scene and asset changes can introduce merge risks. Keep branches small and avoid long-lived diverging branches that accumulate unrelated scene edits. Example workflow: create feature-A branch, add a script and a GameObject, commit, and push. Have a teammate review via a pull request. Once approved, merge into main. Misconception: branching means no coordination required — false. For scene edits, communicate which scenes you will modify, or lock scenes temporarily if your team prefers serialized single-writer access. When merging, if a scene conflict appears, prefer using UnityYAMLMerge or open Unity and reapply the intended changes. Also, write clear commit messages that explain why the change was made; that makes conflict resolution and code review far easier. Takeaway: branches and frequent commits reduce the blast radius of mistakes and make merges tractable for Unity projects. Feature-Branch Workflow for Unity Teams means use short-lived feature branches, frequent commits, and clear messages; coordinate scene edits to reduce conflicts.. In practical terms, branch, commit, review, and merge with minimal disruption. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Branching guidance
keyIdea.text: Use short-lived feature branches, frequent commits, and clear messages; coordinate scene edits to reduce conflicts.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Feature-Branch Workflow
Standard Steps
  1. Create a branch for each feature.
  2. Make focused changes and commit frequently.
  3. Push the branch and open a pull request for review.
  4. Merge after review and tests pass.
For Unity, also communicate scene edits and consider breaking large scenes into smaller scenes or use additive scenes to minimize conflicts.
Practical example
Create branch feature-A, add FeatureA.cs, attach to a GameObject, save scene, commit, push, open pull request. Reviewer checks scene YAML for unexpected edits and approves.
Common mistake
Long-lived branches that diverge from main cause larger merge conflicts. Rebase or merge main frequently to keep branches current.
Key Takeaway

Keep branches small and well communicated; pull requests plus small commits reduce conflict scope for Unity scenes and assets.

screens.title: Resolving Merge Conflicts in Scenes and Prefabs
screens.subtitle: Practical strategies and UnityYAMLMerge configuration

narration.text: Merge conflicts occur when Git cannot automatically reconcile overlapping changes. In Unity, conflicts in. unity and. prefab files are common because multiple developers may edit the same scene. When scenes are serialized as text, you'll see YAML diffs and sometimes conflict markers. A safe strategy is to use Unity's YAML merge tool, UnityYAMLMerge, configured as Git's merge driver. That tool knows Unity's YAML structure and reduces risky manual edits. If you do see conflict markers in a scene file, avoid blindly editing YAML unless you are comfortable with the format. A practical way to resolve is to pick one branch's version to restore the scene, open it in Unity, then manually reapply the missing changes in the editor so Unity updates GUIDs and references correctly. Example: merge feature-B into main and encounter conflict: accept main's camera transform, then reopen Unity and add feature-B's new GameObject back in the editor to preserve integrity. Misconception: manual text merges are always faster — not when YAML references and GUIDs are involved. Always verify the scene in Unity after resolution. Takeaway: prefer UnityYAMLMerge or editor-based reapplication and commit the final scene once you confirm in Unity.

keyIdea.title: Conflict resolution
keyIdea.text: Prefer UnityYAMLMerge or editor reapplication; avoid manual YAML merges unless you understand Unity's structure.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Resolving Merge Conflicts
Strategies
  • Configure UnityYAMLMerge as Git's merge tool when possible.
  • If a conflict appears, avoid manual YAML merges unless you understand GUIDs and references.
  • Prefer restoring one branch's scene and reapplying the other branch's changes inside Unity.
Example resolution flow
  1. Merge feature branch; detect conflict in Assets/Scenes/MyScene.unity.
  2. Choose main's scene as base, open in Unity to confirm.
  3. Recreate or reapply the other branch's additions in the editor and save.
  4. Commit the resolved scene from Unity.
Common mistakes
Editing YAML conflict markers without understanding GUIDs can break references and produce corrupted scenes. Always verify in Unity.
Key Takeaway

Resolve scene conflicts using Unity-aware tools or editor reapplication. Validate the scene in Unity before committing.

screens.title: Simulating a Merge Conflict: Step-by-Step
screens.subtitle: A reproducible exercise to practice resolving a Unity scene conflict

narration.text: This hands-on simulation shows the complete cycle: set up Git and Unity settings, create two branches that change the same scene, and resolve the resulting conflict. Start by initializing Git in your project and committing a clean state with. gitignore. Enable Visible Meta Files and Force Text in Project Settings. Optionally install Git LFS and track common file types. Next, create branch feature-A, add a script and an empty GameObject, place it at position 1,0,0, save the scene, and commit. Switch to main, create branch feature-B, add a different GameObject at -1,0,0, save and commit. Modify the camera on main and commit. Merge feature-A into main first — it should merge cleanly. Then merge feature-B into main; you will likely see a conflict in the scene file. Open the conflicted. unity file in a text editor to observe conflict markers, but resolve the conflict by opening the scene in Unity: choose the camera position you prefer, re-add any missing GameObjects, save, and commit the resolved scene. This exercise demonstrates why Force Text and. meta tracking are crucial and why small, focused commits make conflict resolution clearer. After resolving, open the scene to verify all objects and transforms are present.

keyIdea.title: Practice flow
keyIdea.text: Reproduce a conflict via two branches, then resolve using Unity editor actions to learn safe merge techniques.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Simulating a Merge Conflict
Activity Steps (Terminal-first)
Init & Settings
git init → add .gitignore → commit. Set Visible Meta Files and Force Text in Unity.
Configure LFS (optional)
git lfs install → git lfs track "*.png" "*.fbx" → commit .gitattributes
Branch A
git checkout -b feature-A → add GameObject at (1,0,0) → commit
Branch B
git checkout main → git checkout -b feature-B → add GameObject at (-1,0,0) → commit
Merge and Resolve
Merge feature-A then feature-B into main. If conflict occurs, open the scene in Unity, choose the correct camera transform, reapply missing objects, save, and commit the resolved scene.
Try this
After resolution, open the scene and confirm Feature A and Feature B GameObjects are present and camera is correct.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Best Practices
screens.subtitle: Avoid pitfalls and adopt practices that scale across teams

narration.text: Teams often make a handful of recurring mistakes when using Git with Unity. A major mistake is committing generated folders like Library/, which instantly bloats the repo and creates machine-specific conflicts. Another is failing to enable Visible Meta Files and Force Text early, which makes later merges extremely difficult. A third is adding Git LFS after large files already exist in history; this doesn't shrink past history. Contrast these failures with best practices: create and commit. gitignore immediately, set Unity editor serialization to Force Text and Visible Meta Files, plan LFS rules up front and commit. gitattributes, and use short-lived feature branches with frequent commits. Example: a team that sets these rules from project start will have smaller clones, more meaningful diffs, and fewer broken references. Misconception: you can rely on ad-hoc fixes after problems appear — in reality some fixes require rewriting history and coordination. Practical tips: keep commits focused, write descriptive commit messages, and coordinate scene edits or break scenes into smaller additive scenes. Takeaway: prevention through configuration and small commits beats reactive fixes every time. Common Mistakes and Best Practices means set .gitignore and unity serialization early, plan lfs, and commit small changes to minimize future pain.. In practical terms, avoid pitfalls and adopt practices that scale across teams. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Preventive practices
keyIdea.text: Set .gitignore and Unity serialization early, plan LFS, and commit small changes to minimize future pain.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Common Mistakes vs Best Practices
Common Mistakes
  • Committing Library/ or Temp/ and inflating repo size.
  • Leaving serialization in Binary, preventing meaningful diffs.
  • Adding LFS after large files already exist in history.
Best Practices
  • Create .gitignore and commit it before adding assets.
  • Enable Visible Meta Files and Force Text immediately.
  • Plan Git LFS rules and commit .gitattributes early.
  • Use feature branches and small commits for scene edits.
Key Takeaway

Preventive configuration and communication save time. Fixing tracked binaries later is expensive.

screens.subtitle: Commit strategies that make history useful and efficient

narration.text: Good commit hygiene makes project history a useful audit trail. Commit small, self-contained changes with messages that explain intent, not just what files changed. For Unity, commit logical units such as a script plus a small scene change together, rather than dumping many unrelated changes into a single commit. Avoid committing large binaries directly; use Git LFS instead. When you must remove tracked large files from history, coordinate with your team because rewriting history affects everyone and requires a forced push. Example strategy: for a gameplay feature, commit the script and the small scene tweak in a single branch, open a pull request that includes the YAML diff for reviewers to inspect, and merge once approved. Misconception: frequent small commits clutter history — in fact they make it easier to bisect and revert. Also keep branches rebased or merged often so your branch doesn't diverge extensively. Takeaway: write commits for humans: explain why the change was needed, include testing notes in the message, and keep commits narrow so future merges and rollbacks are straightforward. Commit Hygiene
Treat each commit as a single logical step. Use messages that explain why, include brief testing notes, and keep related changes grouped together.
Good
Add jump script + update jump prefab + unit test. Message explains behavior and test steps.

Key Takeaway

Clear, small commits make review, bisecting, and merges far easier — plan commits around intent, not file count.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: These are the core concepts to keep in mind. First, a Version Control System records file changes over time; Git's distributed model means each developer has a full history for offline work and flexible branching. Second, a correct Unity setup requires Visible Meta Files and Force Text so scenes and prefabs serialize as readable YAML that Git can diff. Third,. gitignore must exclude generated and user-specific files like Library/ and Temp/ to prevent repository bloat. Fourth, Git LFS should be planned and enabled before large assets are added; it stores pointers in Git and keeps binaries on a separate LFS server. Fifth, feature branches and small commits reduce conflict risk, and proper conflict resolution often uses UnityYAMLMerge or reapplying changes in the Unity editor. Keep these ideas together: configuration prevents problems, LFS prevents bloat, and disciplined branching and commits make merges manageable. If you remember these points, you will avoid the most common team-scale failures when using Git with Unity.
